title: Meghan Markle: private-letter publication and the 2019 media wave
subject: Meghan Markle: private-letter publication and the 2019 media wave

source.name: Recovered headline sample
source.scopeNote: Fixed window 2019-02-06 through 2019-02-23 inclusive. Ten dated records: four Guardian publisher pages, five Mail/MailOnline article titles transcribed in paragraph 6 of the 2020 High Court judgment, and one directly verified People context page dated 6 February. Three playable desks remain; People is context-only, not a fourth chart desk. Court records two print headlines and three MailOnline web headlines, all dated 10 February 2019. Secondary commentary also gives 9 February; retain the court date pending original timestamp evidence. The sample does not establish overall volume or trends.
source.sampleNote: 10 records including one People context-only publisher page; chart retains three desks and nine playable/countable records. Five Mail/MailOnline titles are court-transcribed, not direct publisher page recoveries. Print/web distinction preserved; no private letter text.

events.label: People published an article quoting friends and referencing a private letter to Thomas Markle.
The Mail on Sunday and MailOnline published extracts from the handwritten letter.
Reports described potential legal action and Thomas Markle’s response.

Guardian comment discussed press treatment after extracts from the letter had been published.
Guardian comment criticized the scrutiny and vilification directed at Meghan.

evidence.label: Court of Appeal judgment upholding the privacy finding (2021; court file hosted later)
evidence.text: The Court of Appeal upheld the finding that the Duchess had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the letter. The judgment concerns five challenged articles; it is not a ruling on all coverage.

evidence.label: Judiciary case summary
evidence.text: The summary identifies the media context: a People article on 6 February 2019, followed by extracts from the private letter published in the Mail on Sunday on 10 February 2019. The court said the later articles were not a proportionate means of correcting inaccuracies.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2019-02-06
evidence.text: People published an article quoting friends and referencing a private letter to Thomas Markle. It formed the stated context for the publisher’s later claim that its own article answered inaccuracies.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2019-02-10
evidence.text: The Mail on Sunday and MailOnline published extracts from the handwritten letter. Publication triggered a privacy dispute; the letter remained personal correspondence.

evidence.label: Public-interest chronology: 2019-02-11
evidence.text: Reports described potential legal action and Thomas Markle’s response. At this stage litigation was contemplated, not yet adjudicated.

evidence.label: High Court strike-out ruling dated 1 May 2020 (retrospective)
evidence.text: The High Court struck three categories of pleaded allegation about dishonesty or bad faith, stirring up father–daughter conflict and an alleged agenda to publish intrusive or damaging stories. This procedural ruling did not determine substantive privacy or copyright liability. Copyright was not in issue on this application; the substantive summary judgment came on 11 February 2021.

evidence.label: An early letter and family-rift report is promoted · original X post

The current profile displays Mail+; the 2019 display name was not recovered. The link resolves to a Mail news page, but this post is not evidence that the five later challenged articles were already published. No private letter text is reproduced.

evidence.label: Privacy and copyright summary judgment · 2021-02-11
evidence.text: The court granted summary judgment on misuse of private information and on copyright subsistence and infringement. A limited copyright co-authorship issue remained open. The decision concerns the challenged letter articles, not all reporting about Markle or a numerical threshold for acceptable coverage.

evidence.label: Publication of a copyright notice ordered · 2021-03-05
evidence.text: The court set terms for print and online notices reporting its copyright finding. The May judgment records that publication was stayed pending an appeal application. An order is not proof the notice appeared on that date, and a court notice is not a voluntary apology. The remaining ownership issue and later appeal must retain their own dates.

evidence.label: Final copyright liability and account of profits · 2021-05-12
evidence.text: The court resolved the remaining ownership issue in Markle’s favour, entered final summary judgment on copyright liability and gave directions for an account of profits. This did not quantify the profits or decide all privacy financial remedies. It confirms an article-specific legal result rather than a finding about the entire news cycle.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would say readers had an interest in a public figure’s family dispute and in the father’s response to an earlier account. The court record lists two print headlines from 10 February transcribed in High Court judgment paragraph 6 (PDF pp. 2–3). These are transcriptions from a later judgment, not recovered publisher pages or a census of our output.

One headline called the correspondence a “tragedy” and foregrounded a rift; the other paired a plea with the father’s response. We could argue that competing accounts served the public. But status alone does not make private correspondence public, especially when less intrusive reporting could explain the dispute.

At publication, the publisher argued the letter corrected inaccuracies and readers deserved the father’s reply. Those were contested claims. Later, the High Court and Court of Appeal found the five specified articles unlawful on privacy grounds; most disclosures were not a proportionate correction. A defence must acknowledge that result.

The complete sample has ten records, including one context-only People web page dated 6 February; the playable chart remains three desks. The five Mail/MailOnline titles are a court-confirmed 10 February record, not recovered original pages. Secondary commentary also gives 9 February, so we preserve that uncertainty rather than silently changing the court date. No private letter is reproduced.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend telling readers about the letter dispute and the father’s response, with the earlier People account as context. The court record lists three online headlines from 10 February. We have not recovered those original pages: these exact titles come from a later judgment and do not represent all our output.

Two titles repeat a broken-heart phrase; one uses a handwriting-based character label. We could argue that readers wanted the father’s reply and context. Yet a public figure’s status does not make private family correspondence public property. The character label risks judging personality instead of clarifying the dispute.

The publisher argued at the time that reporting corrected inaccuracies and gave the father a response. These were contested claims, not findings. The later High Court and Court of Appeal found the five challenged pieces unlawful on privacy grounds and the disclosures mostly disproportionate. That result weakens a correction-only defence.

The complete sample has ten records, including one context-only People web page dated 6 February; the playable chart remains three desks. The five Mail/our online desk titles are a court-confirmed 10 February record, not recovered original pages. Secondary commentary also gives 9 February, so we preserve that uncertainty rather than silently changing the court date. No private letter is reproduced.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend the 23 February report as coverage of a legal threat, not a court ruling. On 13 February, we also reported George Clooney’s criticism of press pursuit and publication of a daughter’s letter. Both items addressed public debate about reporting and legal rights, not the family dispute itself.

Our 16 February comment criticized the release of letter extracts; the 20 February column examined how both ordinary and grand gestures drew judgment. We would say scrutiny of that pattern served readers. Commentary still needs evidence and care: a person should not become a symbol or an invitation to judge her character.

Four recovered items span three dates, but this selection cannot show how often we covered Meghan. We would distinguish news from opinion and avoid counting each item as a separate event. The five challenged titles documented by the court belong to another publisher and are not a complete media count.

The complete sample has ten records, including one context-only People web page dated 6 February; the playable chart remains three desks. The five Mail/MailOnline titles are a court-confirmed 10 February record, not recovered original pages. Secondary commentary also gives 9 February, so we preserve that uncertainty rather than silently changing the court date. No private letter is reproduced.

mediaScope.method: Recovered media samples are separate from the written inventory. Hosting-page dates, uploads, podcast releases and broadcast slots have distinct meanings. One programme may have several broadcasts or clips; these are distribution events, not automatically independent reports. Current view counters are dated observations, not unique audiences or campaign-period reach. Similar timing/framing or ideological alignment does not establish payments, direction, motive or foreign coordination.
mediaScope.financingOrCoordinationEvidence: Not established by this collection. Ownership, guest affiliation or repeated framing alone is insufficient.

mediaScope.socialPostRecovery: Selected original contributing posts and counter-speech are distinguished; archived and reported sources retain their own date basis. This is not an X census or complete repost graph. Current counters cannot reconstruct historical reach.

editorialScope.method: Supplemental editorial audit, separate from the fixed headline counts. Linked records are already counted; unmatched items are additional context, not a revised census. Aftermath is excluded from the selected window. Unsigned leaders show institutional positions; bylined opinion shows its author’s position. No direct owner statement or direction has been established.
editorialScope.gaps: No qualifying record recovered here does not establish that an outlet published no editorials. Original Sun leader page and a complete cross-outlet editorial census remain gaps.

attentionScope.method: Written records, contributing posts, counter-speech, editorial records and case events share a date axis but keep separate counts. Links are shown only for verified previews, article promotion, quoting or replies. The fixed 179-headline inventory is unchanged.
attentionScope.limits: Recovered examples do not measure all exposure or establish that every item was a pile-on. Present counters and historical snapshots have different dates and cannot be joined into an assumed growth curve.
attentionScope.gaps: No qualifying contributing X post recovered for Jefferies. Other cases contain selected examples, not complete platform samples. Deleted posts and missing captures remain recovery gaps.

accountabilityRecords.title: A procedural ruling, before the merits decision
accountabilityRecords.summary: The court struck three pleaded categories of allegation. Copyright was not in issue on this application.
accountabilityRecords.limit: This did not decide whether the letter publication infringed privacy or copyright. The earlier bundle description of this ruling as substantive summary judgment has been corrected.

accountabilityRecords.title: Privacy and copyright summary judgment
accountabilityRecords.summary: The court granted summary judgment on misuse of private information and on copyright subsistence and infringement. A limited copyright co-authorship issue remained open.
accountabilityRecords.limit: The decision concerns the challenged letter articles, not all reporting about Markle or a numerical threshold for acceptable coverage.

accountabilityRecords.title: Publication of a copyright notice ordered
accountabilityRecords.summary: The court set terms for print and online notices reporting its copyright finding. The May judgment records that publication was stayed pending an appeal application.
accountabilityRecords.limit: An order is not proof the notice appeared on that date, and a court notice is not a voluntary apology. The remaining ownership issue and later appeal must retain their own dates.

accountabilityRecords.title: Final copyright liability and account of profits
accountabilityRecords.summary: The court resolved the remaining ownership issue in Markle’s favour, entered final summary judgment on copyright liability and gave directions for an account of profits.
accountabilityRecords.limit: This did not quantify the profits or decide all privacy financial remedies. It confirms an article-specific legal result rather than a finding about the entire news cycle.

accountabilityRecords.title: The appeal tests proportionate publication
accountabilityRecords.summary: The appeal upheld the privacy outcome concerning five challenged articles. The court concluded that publication was not a proportionate response to the People article.
accountabilityRecords.limit: This is a later legal finding about identified publications. It does not adjudicate every outlet’s coverage or disclose what editors knew at every earlier stage.

accountabilityScope.rule: Later findings have their own dates and scope. They are excluded from the headline counts and do not establish what an editor knew at first publication. An institution’s account, a reported finding and a court judgment are different kinds of evidence.
accountabilityScope.gaps: Samples remain uneven. Complete daily social reach, full broadcast transcripts, earlier page versions and a consistently measured comparator have not been recovered for every case.
